text: Wilhelm Fabry (also known as William Fabry, Guilelmus Fabricius Hildanus, or Fabricius von Hilden) (25 June 1560 – 15 February 1634) is commonly referred to as the "Father of German surgery" and was the first educated and scientific German surgeon. He is one of the most prominent figures in the iatromechanics school and authored 20 medical books. His posthumous publication, Observationum et Curationum Chirurgicarum Centuriae (1641), remains the best collection of surgical case records of the century, offering clear insight into the range and methods of his practice. Fabry developed innovative surgical techniques and created new surgical instruments.[1] He also wrote a significant treatise on burns.[2][3] Born in Hilden, he became Badergeselle ('surgeon's mate') in Düsseldorf in 1579 under the court surgeon Cosmas Slot. In 1587, he married Marie Colinet (or Fabry), daughter of Eustache Colinet, a Genevese printer; she was a Swiss midwife–surgeon who advanced cesarean section techniques. She assisted her husband in surgery and, in 1624, became the first person to use a magnet to extract metal from a patient's eye—a method still in use today. Fabry documented the procedure in his Centuriae, though he explicitly credited his wife as the inventor, he was credited for the discovery. From 1602 to 1615, he served as a city surgeon in Payerne and Lausanne, Switzerland, and was later appointed city surgeon (Stadtarzt) of Bern by the city council, a position he held until his death. The city of Bern, where he died, named a street after him (Hildanusstrasse), using a Latin version of his name. His birthplace, Hilden, named a city museum featuring surgical instruments and related items after him, installed a bronze bust of him in the market place, and named streets after both him and his wife.
